notes.claim: Zs = Ze + (R1+R2): Ze is the external impedance of the supply and R1+R2 the circuit's own line and protective conductor resistance, which grows with length.
Calculated R1+R2 is (mΩ/m) × multiplier × length / 1000; the slides' 1.5 mm² line and cpc at 24.2 mΩ/m, multiplier 1.2 and 15 m gives 0.43 Ω, and Zs 0.64 Ω with Ze 0.21 Ω.
Loop impedance is limited because a lower Zs lets a higher fault current flow, which operates the device within the required time; the slides find 341.4 A at Cmin 0.95.
Cmin is the minimum voltage factor allowing for supply voltage variation, 0.95 for a low voltage supply under the ESQCR; the slides explain 230 V can fall to 218.5 V.
Final circuits to 32 A must disconnect in accordance with Table 41.1 (0.4 s in the slides' TN example), and these are maximum disconnection times, not actual ones.
Cmin is best used when deciding the fault current that operates a protective device, and Cmax and Cmin are not used together but in separate calculations.

Zs = Ze + (R1+R2), where R1+R2 is the tabulated milliohms per metre x the multiplier x the length / 1000 (formula sheet, step 12). The On-Site Guide's Table I1 values are at 20 °C, and Table I3's multiplier brings them to the conductors' operating temperature, which the limiting Zs values assume.

For the showroom motor's supply cable (2.5 mm² line and 2.5 mm² cpc, 90 °C thermosetting singles in conduit) the On-Site Guide's Table I1 gives 14.82 mΩ/m and Table I3 gives the multiplier 1.28 for a conductor in a cable or bunched (1.04 where it is neither); the 4 mm² and 6 mm² rows read 9.22 and 6.16 mΩ/m, for changed-numbers work.

The device's maximum Zs comes from its fault current: Table 41.3's values are calculated from the Regulation 411.4.4 formula with the current that opens the device in the time (Appendix 3), a type C breaker trips instantaneously at 5 to 10 times In and the table uses the worst case, so a 25 A type C is 0.87 ohm at 0.4 s (230 x 0.95 / 250 = 0.874 ohm, rounded down). Designers should use the maker's data where there is some.

The calculated Zs is compared with the tabulated maximum, which is the limit when the conductors are hot; a reading taken cold is compared with the On-Site Guide's measured values instead (80% of the tabulated, so 0.7 ohm for a 25 A type C), which is lesson 9's business.

The course's own framing: the circuit works as a circuit before its shock risk is judged; Zs must not exceed the device's maximum for the required time; in the slides' heater the fault current clears the device's Ia of 80 A, so it disconnects in 0.1 s against the 0.4 s allowed.

Which time applies: Table 41.1's maximum times (0.4 s on a 230 V TN supply) apply to final circuits up to 32 A, and up to 63 A if they supply socket-outlets (Regulation 411.3.2.2); distribution circuits and other final circuits may take up to 5 s under 411.3.2.3 (and these are maximums, not actual times).

When Zs is too high the designer can reduce R1+R2 (larger line or cpc, or a shorter run), change the device type (a type B passes a longer run than a type C), or add an RCD. This is a trade site's list, not a regulation.

An RCD needs far less of an earth path than an overcurrent device: its Zs limits (Table 41.5, from the 50 V condition of Regulation 411.5.3) are in the hundreds or thousands of ohms, and RCDs provided for fault protection are covered by Regulation 411.4.204. It does not remove the need to check Zs: a high reading can mean a loose connection.

Where the disconnection times cannot be met, supplementary protective equipotential bonding is the other route (IEC 60364-4-41 411.3.2.6 and 415.2, which BS 7671 follows); it is contested whether it limits the touch voltage to 50 V when the time is relaxed to 1 s or 5 s.

An EV charging point on a TN-C-S (PME) supply: the final circuit must not include a PEN conductor, and a PME earthing facility must not be used as the earth of an outdoor charging point unless one of the Regulation 722.411.4.1 methods is used (each rests on the earth-to-main-earthing-terminal voltage staying at or below 70 V rms in an open-circuit PEN fault): balanced loading on a three-phase installation, an earth electrode, or an open-PEN detection device. An RCD does not protect against that fault.

EV RCD protection (Regulation 722.531.3.101): a 30 mA RCD per charging point, with protection against DC residual current by a Type B RCD or a Type A or F with a residual direct-current detecting device (6 mA), unless the charging equipment provides it; the RCD protects the charging point rather than the circuit; the course's guide asks the designer to be mindful of it.
